consensus: DeepSeek V4 is presented as an open-weight foundation model with native multimodal input for text, images, and video.
It is strongly associated with very long-context use, including a context window of over one million tokens.
The sources frame it as useful for long-document analysis, large codebases, extended agent traces, and other workflows where broad context matters.
Its architecture is described as aiming to reduce attention and cache costs at very long sequence lengths, which makes inference economics a central part of the story.
The evidence consistently treats it as a live, serious competitor in the open or semi-open model ecosystem.

context_card.use_this_page_when: Use this page when deciding whether DeepSeek V4 is a good fit for multimodal, long-context, self-hosted, or cost-sensitive AI workflows, especially if you are comparing open-weight deployment options.

evidence_quality: Evidence is split across three sources, with one source being more promotional in tone and two providing architecture-oriented secondary coverage.
The strongest claims about performance are benchmark-style numbers, but no testing methodology or evaluator details are provided in the sources.
Long-context efficiency claims are more concrete than the raw benchmark claims, because the architecture article reports specific FLOPs and KV-cache reductions at 1M tokens.
Real-world maturity is suggested by repeated coverage and open-weight availability, but there are no adoption metrics or production failure analyses.
executive_synthesis: DeepSeek V4 is best understood as an open-weight, multimodal model built for long-context and cost-sensitive inference. The sources agree that it can handle text, images, and video, and that its very large context window makes it relevant for long documents, large codebases, extended agent traces, and other workflows where keeping everything in one prompt matters. The main technical story is efficiency: one source describes architectural changes aimed at reducing attention and cache cost at long sequence lengths, and another reports large reductions in FLOPs and KV-cache usage at 1M tokens relative to earlier DeepSeek variants. That makes it interesting for teams that want self-hosted control and lower direct cloud-token spend. However, the evidence on benchmark performance is mostly announcement-style and lacks methodology, and the sources do not give enough detail on latency, memory footprint, or operational burden to treat it as proven production-ready without local validation.

practical_example.example: A support team wants one model to review a customer case that includes a long chat history, screenshots, and a short screen-recording clip. DeepSeek V4 is relevant here because the sources describe native text/image/video support and a 1M+ token context window. In practice, that means the team could keep the whole case together instead of splitting it across separate OCR, vision, and summarization steps. If they self-host, they may also avoid per-token cloud pricing. The open question is whether their actual serving stack can handle the memory and latency demands of a very large multimodal model.

practical_takeaway: Consider DeepSeek V4 when the workflow is dominated by long context, mixed media, and a desire to self-host. Validate serving cost, latency, and reliability before relying on it in production.
tensions: The sources imply strong benchmark performance, but they do not provide enough methodology to verify the math/coding numbers.
The model is framed as cheaper to use when self-hosted, but total cost is not established because hardware, ops, and maintenance are not quantified.
Architecture-oriented coverage suggests meaningful long-context efficiency gains, but it is unclear how much comes from the architecture alone versus the full training and system recipe.
The model is described as having impressive agentic capabilities, but the sources do not explain failure modes or whether those capabilities hold up in production.
title: DeepSeek V4
what_to_remember: Open-weight and self-hostable, which matters if data control or internal deployment is a priority.
Native multimodal support spans text, images, and video.
The >1M token context window is the most operationally important feature for large documents and extended agent traces.
Long-context efficiency is a core claim: the architecture is meant to cut attention and cache cost at very long sequence lengths.
Benchmark numbers are present, but they are not independently validated in the sources.
Useful for workflow simplification, but not enough evidence here to skip local serving and reliability tests.
